The bucium is an alphorn-type instrument of Romania and Moldova, a lip-vibrated aerophone of the horn and brass class, Hornbostel–Sachs 423.121.11. Its tube may be straight or curved, with either the whole length or only the bell conical; it measures from 1.5 to 3 metres or more and is mostly made of spruce, ash, lime or hazel, bound with birch, cherry or lime bark; northern Romanian versions may contain metal. The player sounds it by blowing into a horn-shaped wooden mouthpiece. Traditionally it was used by mountain dwellers, soldiers and shepherds for signals, for communication in forest and mountain, for guiding sheep and dogs, and at funerals.
布奇烏姆號為羅馬尼亞與摩爾多瓦的阿爾卑斯號類型，其名源自拉丁文，原指羅馬人使用的: The bucium is an alphorn type of Romania and Moldova. Its name comes from Latin, where it first meant the curved horn the Romans used, and it is akin to English 'cornet'. Romanian documents mention it from at least the sixteenth century. Traditionally it was used by mountain people, soldiers and shepherds for signals, for communication in forest and mountain, and for guiding flocks and dogs, and it was also heard at funerals. Under the name trembita it is played as well by the Hutsuls of Ukraine and the Gorals of Poland.

A related instrument is known as the trembita, whose sound differs from the ordinary alphorn's; the same name is used too among the Hutsuls of Ukraine and the Gorals of Poland. The source mentions no specific composers or works.
